passage:
Monday. Akash, two, stood in the middle of the room with both hands over his eyes. "Akash gone!" Jahnavi, his mother, laughed. "I can see you!" He peeked, frowned, and pressed his hands on harder.
Thursday. He held up his picture book to show her the duck, but the page faced his own nose. "Look, Amma!" She could see only the back cover.
Ten days later. He hid his face in the curtain again. This time Jahnavi just smiled and asked the room, "Where did Akash go?"

qa.q: What did Akash cover his eyes with on Monday?
qa.a: Both hands.

qa.q: Why does Akash believe he is gone when his eyes are covered?
qa.a: Akash feels safely hidden and pleased, because when he can't see anyone it seems nobody can see him; at two he can't yet picture the room from his mother's side.

qa.q: What choice did Jahnavi make ten days later, and why did it suit Akash's age?
qa.a: She stopped telling him she could see him and joined the game instead, so it stayed fun while his sense of other views grows in its own time.

qa.q: What is it like for Jahnavi when Akash shows her the book?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees only the back cover and has to guess what he means, even though to Akash the duck is plainly on show.

grounding: A two-year-old covers his eyes to vanish and shows a book facing himself, not yet able to imagine his mother's view.

subtype: My view is the only view [Actor]
passage:
The lift in the Pune apartment block stopped on the fourth floor, and Chinmay from the flat upstairs stepped in with a loaf of bread. Thomas, almost three, buried his face in his father's shoulder. "Thomas not here," he announced into the shirt.
Chinmay grinned. "Oh no. Where has Thomas gone?"
Thomas stayed perfectly still, only his sandals kicking. When the doors opened on the ground floor, he lifted his head and shouted, "Here I am!" as if he had been far away.

qa.q: Where did Thomas bury his face?
qa.a: In his father's shoulder.

qa.q: Why does Thomas think saying 'Thomas not here' makes him hidden?
qa.a: Thomas feels safely hidden and shy, because with his face in the shirt he sees nobody; he can't yet imagine that Chinmay still has a full view of him.

qa.q: Which choice did Chinmay make when Thomas hid, and why did it work?
qa.a: Chinmay played along and asked where Thomas had gone, so the little boy felt his game worked instead of being corrected about something he can't yet understand.

qa.q: How might Thomas's father see this lift ride?
qa.a: He knows his son is in full view the whole time, and probably finds it sweet that the hiding feels so real to Thomas.

grounding: A toddler hides his face in a lift and announces he is not there, sure that not seeing means not being seen.

subtype: My view is the only view [Actor]
passage:
"Wasim bhai, see my drawing!" Suraj, three, held the paper up high, crayon side toward his own nose.
"I only see white paper, Suraj."
"No, look! Big truck!"
"Turn it round?"
Suraj pulled the paper closer to his face. "Big truck, see?"
Ammi called from the kitchen, "Show me too, jaan."
Suraj ran in and held it up the same way. "Truck, Ammi!"
"A truck! What colour is it?"
"Red!"
Wasim came and stood behind his little brother, looked over his shoulder, and laughed. "Oh, it IS a big truck."

qa.q: What had Suraj drawn?
qa.a: A big red truck.

qa.q: Why does Suraj keep insisting that Wasim can see the truck?
qa.a: Suraj feels excited and sure: he can see the truck himself, so he assumes anyone looking at the paper sees it too, not yet realising the other side is just white paper.

qa.q: What choice finally let Wasim see the drawing, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: Wasim stood behind Suraj and looked over his shoulder, meeting the little boy where he was instead of arguing about which way the paper faced.

qa.q: How does Ammi handle not being able to see the drawing?
qa.a: Ammi asks what colour the truck is, so she shares Suraj's excitement without needing to see the page 😊

grounding: A three-year-old shows his drawing facing himself to his brother and mother, sure they can see what he sees.

passage: Daycare note, Monday. At tidy-up time Veer (2) crouched behind the curtain, but his feet and bottom stuck out. When I called, "Where's Veer?" he pressed his hands over his eyes and giggled, sure he was hidden. Later he held up his drawing to show me, with the picture facing his own nose. I saw only the blank back. I turned it round and said, "Now I can see it!" He looked puzzled, then turned it back to himself. — Aparna

qa.q: What stuck out from behind the curtain?
qa.a: Veer's feet and bottom.

qa.q: Why did Veer giggle with his hands over his eyes?
qa.a: Veer felt delighted and sure he was hidden, believing that because he couldn't see anyone, nobody could see him.

qa.q: What did Aparna do to help Veer notice another view, and what could Aparna keep doing?
qa.a: Aparna turned the drawing round and said "Now I can see it!", and can keep playing such games so he slowly learns others see differently.

qa.q: What does Aparna see that Veer can't yet imagine?
qa.a: Aparna sees his feet sticking out and the blank back of his drawing, while Veer assumes everyone sees what he sees.

grounding: A caregiver notes a toddler who covers his eyes to hide and shows a picture facing himself, unable to imagine another view.

passage: In the courtyard of their house near Kottayam, Tomy, two, heard his mother, Elizabeth, calling him for his bath. He squeezed his eyes shut and stood very still beside the coconut pile. "Tomy gone," he announced. His sister Anjali laughed. "I can see you!" Tomy shut his eyes tighter. Then he held up a shell to show Anjali, the shiny side toward his own face. "See? Pretty!" Anjali saw only its rough grey back.

qa.q: What did Tomy announce with his eyes shut?
qa.a: "Tomy gone."

qa.q: Why did Tomy shut his eyes tighter when Anjali said she could see him?
qa.a: Tomy felt determined to stay hidden; to him hiding meant not seeing, so squeezing his eyes harder seemed like hiding better.

qa.q: How could Anjali gently show Tomy what she sees?
qa.a: She could turn the shell round toward herself and say "Now I see the shiny side!", making a simple game of it.

qa.q: What is it like for Anjali when Tomy shows her the shell?
qa.a: She is shown only a rough grey back while Tomy is sure she sees the pretty side, which is funny and a little puzzling for her.

grounding: A toddler shuts his eyes to hide and shows a shell facing himself, not yet imagining that others see differently.
